The House of Scion · Colour Study

The Twelve Palettes
Second Edition

The same system as before: four skin depths, three undertones, five best colours, five highly acceptable colours and ten combinations for each profile. It is rebuilt from the classic colours of tailoring and couture cloth, and every colour is measured against the complexion it is meant to flatter. The second edition is now live on the Skin Profile page. Below, each first-edition palette sits beside its replacement, with the reasoning and the measurements.

Scorecard · all twelve palettes

TestFirst editionSecond edition
Colours that melt into the skin they are meant forΔE00 below 10 from the skin reference: the garment reads as nude and the face loses definition130
Screen-neon colourschroma C* above 65: highlighter-bright on a monitor, hard to dye and match consistently on natural fibre240
Near-copies inside one palettetwo named colours within ΔE00 8 of each other: one slot wasted130
Combination colours not in the palettea pairing uses a colour the client was never given as a single900
Palettes without a dark groundno navy, charcoal, chocolate or black-level colour: no suit, trouser or coat colour100
Palettes without a light groundno white, ivory, ecru or cream for shirting and linings40
Off-undertone coloursgolden colours in a cool palette, or icy colours in a warm one00

How the new palettes were built

1 · Seasonal colour analysis

Each of the twelve profiles is mapped to its closest family in the twelve-season method used by professional image consultants. Skin depth sets how light or dark the colours are and how much contrast they carry. Undertone sets whether they lean warm or cool. How clear or muted the skin is sets how clean or greyed the colours are.

2 · Timeless fabric colours

Every colour is one with a long life in cloth: navy, charcoal, camel, ecru, cognac, oxblood, bottle green, bordeaux, emerald, sapphire, saffron. Each is named the way a mill, tailor or atelier would name it, so it can be sourced and re-ordered season after season.

3 · Heroes and grounds

Best colours are the heroes, worn close to the face. Highly acceptable colours are the grounds a wardrobe is built on. Every palette now has a light ground (white, ivory, ecru or cream) and a dark ground (navy, charcoal, chocolate, black or forest), so a suit, a shirt and a coat can all be cut from one palette.

4 · Measured against the skin

Every colour is checked with CIEDE2000, the same maths the Colourist uses to match fabric. No colour sits within ΔE 10 of its skin reference. Closer than that and the garment melts into the complexion: the face loses definition and the outfit reads as nude.

5 · Cloth-real saturation

No colour goes above chroma C* 62. The first edition used screen colours such as #FFD60A, #8020C8 and #2ECC71, which glow on a monitor but cannot be dyed consistently on cotton, silk or wool, and which look costume-like in cloth.

6 · Combinations from the palette

Every pairing uses only that palette's own ten colours. The client is never shown a combination built from a colour they were not given, and the Colourist can match every half of every combination to real fabric.

How to read the page: a red outline on a swatch means it fails at least one test, and the reason is written under it. A dashed outline on half of a combination means that colour is not in the palette. In the drape test, each colour is a square of cloth with the skin reference laid on it, the way a colourist holds fabric under a client's chin. Where the disc disappears into the cloth, the colour is too close to the skin.

Fair / Light Skin · cool undertone

Closest seasonal family: Light Summer · skin reference #EBD4CB

Reading the client

Light skin with pink or blue undertones and little contrast between skin, hair and eyes. Strong black and hard primaries overpower it; golden colours turn it sallow.

The hero colours

Powder Blue, Rose Quartz and Heather Lilac are pastels with grey in them, the way they come out of silk crepe de chine and fine cotton voile. Mulberry is the one deep accent: a blue-red that keeps the cheeks rosy. Slate Navy replaces black as the dark colour.

The grounds

Chalk White, not optic white. Dove Grey and Pewter for suiting. Eucalyptus adds a cool green, which the old palette did not have.

What was wrong with the first edition

  • Near-copies: Dusty Pink is a near-copy of Rose Pink · ΔE 7.6.
  • 5 of 20 combination slots used colours the palette never offered.
  • No dark ground: nothing to cut a suit, trouser or coat in.

Fair / Light Skin · warm undertone

Closest seasonal family: Light Spring · skin reference #EFD6BA

Reading the client

Light, golden, clear. It wants warmth and freshness, but at a light-to-medium weight. Dusty or icy colours make it look tired.

The hero colours

Soft Coral and Apricot are the classic spring warms. Lagoon is a warm aqua, a blue-green that does not chill the skin. Camel is the most enduring warm colour in wool and cashmere. Primrose is a buttery yellow for summer linen and silk.

The grounds

Ivory, never stark white. Marine Navy gives the wardrobe a tailoring colour that the old palette lacked completely. Toffee, Pistachio and Warm Stone are soft bridges.

What was wrong with the first edition

  • Blended into the skin: Cream (ΔE 6.6), Warm Beige (ΔE 2.3), Ivory (ΔE 9.2), Sand (ΔE 8.3).
  • Screen-neon: Warm Red #C83020 (C* 74), Mustard #D8A020 (C* 68).
  • Near-copies: Warm Beige is a near-copy of Cream · ΔE 6.0; Light Terra is a near-copy of Apricot · ΔE 7.0.
  • 9 of 20 combination slots used colours the palette never offered.
  • No dark ground: nothing to cut a suit, trouser or coat in.

Fair / Light Skin · neutral undertone

Closest seasonal family: Soft Summer · skin reference #E8D5C4

Reading the client

Light and balanced, neither pink nor golden. Muted, slightly greyed colours look expensive on it; loud colour wears the person.

The hero colours

Dusty Rose, Sage, Soft Teal, Rosewood and Chambray are the quiet mid-tones found in fine wool jersey, washed silk and cotton shirting.

The grounds

Porcelain, Greige and Mushroom are the classic light-neutral trio. Ink Navy is the dark colour. Dusk Lilac is the soft accent.

What was wrong with the first edition

  • Blended into the skin: White (ΔE 9.7), Light Gray (ΔE 9.6), Beige (ΔE 2.7), Cream (ΔE 9.5).
  • Near-copies: Beige is a near-copy of White · ΔE 7.5; Soft Peach is a near-copy of Blush · ΔE 7.7; Pale Blue is a near-copy of Soft Blue · ΔE 6.3.
  • 6 of 20 combination slots used colours the palette never offered.
  • No dark ground: nothing to cut a suit, trouser or coat in.

Medium / Olive Skin · cool undertone

Closest seasonal family: Cool Summer → True Winter · skin reference #C8977F

Reading the client

Medium depth with a cool, often slightly green-grey cast. Yellow-based colours make olive skin look ashy. Clear, cool jewels at medium depth bring it to life.

The hero colours

Emerald, Sapphire, Aubergine, Raspberry and Petrol are the jewel tones of silk and fine suiting, pitched at medium depth rather than neon.

The grounds

Soft White, Cool Grey and Charcoal are the grounds. Orchid Mist and Steel Blue are the lighter partners.

What was wrong with the first edition

  • Screen-neon: Plum #6A1E90 (C* 70), Magenta #CA0068 (C* 71), Indigo #2A0880 (C* 74).
  • Near-copies: Steel Blue is a near-copy of Slate · ΔE 6.9.
  • 11 of 20 combination slots used colours the palette never offered.
  • No dark ground: nothing to cut a suit, trouser or coat in.
  • No light ground for shirting and linings.

Medium / Olive Skin · warm undertone

Closest seasonal family: True Autumn · skin reference #C99A62

Reading the client

Golden olive skin at medium depth. This is heritage-cloth territory: tweed, cotton drill, block print and suede.

The hero colours

Olive, Terracotta, Deep Teal, Cognac and Antique Mustard. Mustard is deliberately taken deeper than a bright ochre, which sits right on the skin and disappears.

The grounds

Ecru, Khaki, Chocolate, Bottle Green and Oxblood are classic country-and-leather colours that anchor a full wardrobe.

What was wrong with the first edition

  • Blended into the skin: Camel (ΔE 4.1), Sand (ΔE 9.5), Tan (ΔE 0.7).
  • Screen-neon: Golden Yellow #E8A818 (C* 74), Mustard #D8A020 (C* 68), Burnt Orange #C85028 (C* 65).
  • Near-copies: Sand is a near-copy of Warm Beige · ΔE 5.1; Moss Green is a near-copy of Olive · ΔE 3.7.
  • 8 of 20 combination slots used colours the palette never offered.
  • No dark ground: nothing to cut a suit, trouser or coat in.
  • No light ground for shirting and linings.

Tan Skin · cool undertone

Closest seasonal family: True Winter · skin reference #9C6E5C

Reading the client

Deep-medium skin with a cool base. It holds high contrast and saturated cool colour; muddy or golden shades flatten it.

The hero colours

Cobalt, Fuchsia, Royal Purple, Bordeaux and Pine. These are the saturated classics of silk and satin, held to colours cloth can actually carry.

The grounds

Optic White gives crisp contrast at this depth. Charcoal and Midnight Navy are for tailoring. Silver Grey and Icy Mint are the light accents.

  • No light ground for shirting and linings.

Dark / Deep Skin · warm undertone

Closest seasonal family: Deep Autumn · skin reference #53321C

Reading the client

Deep golden or red-brown skin. Rich warm colours and metallic-feeling golds are superb; dark browns sit on the skin and vanish.

The hero colours

Saffron, Copper, Brick Red, Peacock and Olive are warm, rich and at home in silk, brocade and heavy cotton.

The grounds

Cream, Camel and Khaki are the light grounds. Forest replaces dark brown as the dark colour because it contrasts with the skin rather than matching it. Terracotta is the bridge.

What was wrong with the first edition

  • Blended into the skin: Brown (ΔE 2.8).
  • Screen-neon: Gold #FFD60A (C* 86), Brick Red #8B0000 (C* 66), Amber #FF8C00 (C* 84).
  • Near-copies: Soft Brown is a near-copy of Copper · ΔE 6.3; Warm Beige is a near-copy of Cream · ΔE 6.7.
  • 7 of 20 combination slots used colours the palette never offered.
  • No dark ground: nothing to cut a suit, trouser or coat in.

Screen colours are a guide. Before a colour is bought as cloth, it should be confirmed against a physical lab dip or a TCX-standard reference under D65 daylight, since fibre, weave and finish all shift how a dye reads.

Skin references are single representative tones for each profile, taken from the swatches on the Skin Profile page and shifted slightly pinker (cool) or more golden (warm). Real complexions vary within each profile.
